claims.claim: Business-model usage varies, but a widely used framing treats it as the rationale for how an organization creates, delivers, and captures value.
A business model is broader than a revenue model and distinct from a business plan; it connects the offering, stakeholders, delivery, and financial consequences.

Subscription, freemium, affiliate, marketplace, and advertising-supported arrangements are common examples of digital business-model patterns, each involving different exchanges and operating requirements.
Advertising-supported arrangements can provide free content to users while revenue comes from advertisers, so users and payers need not be the same group.
Business-model frameworks are useful but not exhaustive planning tools; external threats and industry analysis can remain outside a canvas representation.
A cost may be analyzed as fixed or variable relative to activity over a stated period; the lesson applies this general accounting distinction without providing a price or projection.

conflictingEvidence.issue: There is no single universally accepted definition or representation of a business model.
positions: OpenStax presents a create-deliver-capture framing and describes the model as a venture design.
OpenLearn emphasizes a conceptual representation of business logic and financial consequences.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson identifies the shared linked-logic idea and explicitly states that usage varies; it does not treat one template as mandatory.
